title: Changelog
html:
Changelog

All notable changes to wikicc are documented in this file.

The format is based on Keep a Changelog, and this project adheres to Semantic Versioning. Entries describe what a user of the binary can observe, not how the change was implemented; the rules behind them live in docs/design.md.

[2.0.1] - 2026-11-09

Fixed

  • Search results and their preview agree: the list is built in reading order, so a hit inside a code block opens at that very block, and the selected row always points at the passage the preview shows.
  • A search hit marks the typed fragment only instead of widening to the whole word: searching read marks read in reader rather than the word. The number of hits is unchanged.

Changed

  • A search result's context line is cut to the width the row really has, so wide characters such as CJK no longer overflow it or end it early; the line follows the panel width and the font size as they change.

[2.0.0] - 2026-11-06

Second release: search becomes a panel with previews, math is typeset, links preview on hover, chapters fold, and a site can be built as a static pages artifact configured by a .wikicc.json.

Added

  • A search panel replaces the sidebar search field. It searches the current document (local) or the whole folder (global), lists one row per occurrence with a one-line context, and previews the passage with every hit marked, including hits inside inline code. Enter opens a result at its place in the article; the arrow keys keep the selected row in sight and survive a scope switch.
  • Math typesetting: inline $…$ and block $$…$$ formulas are rendered with the bundled KaTeX, offline like everything else.
  • Hover previews cover whole documents: a link to another document previews the document, a link to one of its chapters previews that chapter. A preview opens at once with a loading state; when it cannot be built, the panel shows a failure notice with a retry instead of closing. Scrolling inside the preview never scrolls the article underneath.
  • Chapter folding: an arrow beside a heading folds that chapter — and everything nested under it — down to its title, and unfolds it again. The arrows appear when the pointer is on a heading, and folding is never remembered.
  • The pages output format: a static site for an HTTP host such as GitHub Pages. The page carries the reader and a manifest only; each document is a JSON chunk fetched on navigation, and the global search corpus is fetched on first use, so first paint does not grow with the size of the folder.
  • An optional .wikicc.json in the input folder root configures the opening document (home), excluded directories (exclude), the output directory (out), the format, the title and strict; every command-line flag overrides the file. wikicc --init-config writes a starter file without overwriting.
  • --exclude keeps directories out of the site from the command line.
  • Inlined data: asset links open as blob URLs in a new tab.
  • The link graph can switch between the whole folder (global) and the current document's neighbourhood (local).
  • Destinations of inline images and links may contain spaces.

Changed

  • Multi-character CJK queries match consecutive text only: the characters of a query no longer scatter across the document as separate hits.
  • The search preview shows the passage alone, without a title and path banner, and centers the picked hit.
  • The link graph is tighter: the frame adapts to the content, and nodes and labels are smaller.
  • Release archives are named after the system that built them and the architecture: wikicc-ubuntu-amd64-v<version>-<sha>.tar.gz and wikicc-windows-amd64-v<version>-<sha>.zip.

Fixed

  • Reference-style links no longer silently degrade to plain text in citation-dense documents.
  • The search preview lands on the right passage after a hit inside a code block.
  • The search field shows a single clear button: the browser's native clear cross is hidden.
  • The reader's bundled JavaScript and CSS are normalized to LF at build time, so two builds of one input stay byte-identical whatever the checkout's line endings.

[1.0.0] - 2026-11-03

First stable release: the features the reader offers.

Reader

  • Compile a folder of Markdown documents into a self-contained reader that needs no server, no sibling files and no network.
  • Search over titles, headings and body text, including CJK.
  • Link graph of the folder with zoom, pan and drag; a plain left click opens the document of the node.
  • Chapter outline of the current document, following the section being read.
  • Block references: pointing at a chapter of another document previews that chapter, and the preview can be pinned and dragged out of the way. A chapter that does not exist is reported as a broken reference and explained.
  • Tables with sorting and Excel-style per-column filtering.
  • Light and dark themes, and a layout that stays usable down to phone width.

Markdown support

  • GitHub-flavored Markdown: tables, task lists, strikethrough and footnotes.
  • Nested chapters with stable, Unicode-aware heading anchors, so CJK headings keep their text.
  • Chapter links that address one chapter of another document ([label](doc.md#chapter)) or the document as a whole.
  • Reference-style links ([[n]] plus a reference list) alongside ordinary Markdown links, and a reference list rendered for the styles that use it.
  • Fenced code highlighting, done at build time.
  • Mermaid diagrams from a fence tagged mermaid.
  • Raw HTML inside Markdown, passed through unchanged; the input is trusted, so untrusted documents must not be compiled.

Output

  • Two output formats: single-html (one page with everything inlined, opens by double click from any directory) and html-dir (a page plus an assets/ folder, ready to be copied, zipped or served as it is).
  • Assets addressed by content, so identical bytes are stored once no matter how many documents reference them.
  • Nothing is fetched at runtime: no CDN, no web font, no remote stylesheet.
  • Two builds of the same input produce byte-identical artifacts.

Executable

  • One binary with no runtime dependencies: on Windows it carries the project logo as an icon in the file explorer.
  • Statically linked release archives for Linux and Windows, so neither needs runtime packages on the machine that runs it.
